title: Rory of the hill
html_source:
The last lines of the ballad, Rory of the Hill

The poet, and the orator,
The heart of man can sway,
And would to the kind heavens
That Wolfe Tone were here to-day!
Yet trust me friends, dear Ireland’s strength,
Her truest strength is still
The rough-and-ready roving boys,
Like Rory of the Hill.

This may be a central theme of the Cyclops chapter, as it was of Sirens; while the flamboyant, garish language of poets, and the empty rhetoric of oratory can sway, Ireland’s genius and future lie with the best of Irish everyman, at least with those who rise above the type of fecklessness and dissolution exhibited throughout much of Ulysses, and especially in these two chapters, a challenge perhaps as daunting as Odysseus and a few of his faithful Greek “Rapparees” penetrating the walls of Troy.
